agency: Export-Import Bank of the United States
blockers: Statute: EXIM exists under the Export-Import Bank Act and abolition needs legislation or a lapse of the authorization.
Administration and congressional support for reauthorization and for EXIM's critical minerals and industrial base role.

confidence_reason: The Bank's expanded activity and larger budget request, the pending ten-year extension bill and the lack of any EXIM provision in the September continuing resolution were confirmed in CRS, GovInfo bill text and the public law, read for this review. The diverged label reflects the contrast with the abolition essay; Senate and House action after mid-September 2026 was not fully checked.

durability.why: Abolition or reauthorization would be statutory; the current expansion rests on Board decisions and a charter that expires 2026-12-31 unless extended.

est_completion.basis: Inference: the administration's budget request, Board approvals and executive order language all expand EXIM's role, and the only path to abolition is a lapse of the 2026-12-31 authorization that reauthorization bills are meant to prevent.

history.note: Primary-source check: the deciding document was located and read, and an independent reviewer re-rated the record (confidence 76 to 80). The reauthorization status is now backed by (govinfo.gov) the Senate Banking hearing listing, three House Financial Services markup pages and the enrolled H.R. 6500; the absence of an abolition bill still rests on CRS

position: Veronique de Rugy (pp. 717-724), who argues for abolition. The opposing essay by Jennifer Hazelton (pp. 724-727) argues for keeping and using EXIM against China.
proposal: In the chapter's first essay, Veronique de Rugy argues that the Export-Import Bank (EXIM) should be abolished because its financing mostly benefits large firms such as Boeing, does not add net jobs or exports, is not a good deal for taxpayers, and cannot be turned into an effective tool against China. The chapter's second essay, by Jennifer Hazelton (pp. 724-727), takes the opposing view: EXIM should be kept and used as a strategic tool against China's export credit system, lends only where private finance will not, has a low default rate, and returns money to the Treasury. This item tracks de Rugy's abolition position; the actions described below track closer to Hazelton's.
remaining: For abolition as de Rugy proposes, Congress would have to let the charter lapse on 2026-12-31 or repeal it, with existing obligations wound down; the administration's budget and Board activity point the other way.
Congress has not enacted reauthorization; S. 3772 and a House draft are pending and the outcome before 2026-12-31 is unknown.
The chapter's separate suggestion to consider moving EXIM into the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (Commerce chapter, p. 664): no action found.

status_summary: No step toward abolishing EXIM was found. The Bank is operating with a three-member Board (a quorum, per CRS in May 2026) after the Senate confirmed John Jovanovic as President and Chair on 2025-09-18, and it has continued or expanded programs: the Supply Chain Resiliency Initiative for critical minerals, Project Vault (announced 2026-02-02, with an EXIM loan of up to $10 billion approved), its first Make More in America deal, and large-loan notices through August 2026. Executive Order 14415 (2026-07-20) carves EXIM-financed foreign projects and Project Vault out of its restrictions, and the FY2027 budget request raises EXIM's program budget to $200 million from $20 million in FY2026. The Bank's charter and its China and Transformational Exports Program sunset on 2026-12-31; a Senate bill (S. 3772, introduced 2026-02-04 by Sen. Cramer with Sen. Warner, per its GovInfo text) would extend them 10 years and a March 2026 House discussion draft would extend them about five years, and CRS identifies no current bill to abolish the Bank. The continuing appropriations act signed 2026-09-02 (H.R. 6500, Public Law 119-103) contains no EXIM provision.

timeline.event: Senate confirms John Jovanovic as EXIM President and Chair (term to 2029-01-20); the Board has three of five seats filled, enough for a quorum.
Project Vault, a critical minerals reserve, is announced; EXIM's Board approves a direct loan of up to $10 billion for it.

Sen. Cramer, with Sen. Warner as an original cosponsor, introduces S. 3772, the Export-Import Bank Reauthorization Act of 2026, referred to the Senate Banking Committee; its only changes are date amendments that extend the Bank's authority from 2026 to 2036, its loan, guarantee and insurance authority date from 2027 to 2037, and the China and Transformational Exports Program dates from 2026 to 2036.

A House discussion draft (March 2026; exact day not given) would extend the Bank's sunset, the China and Transformational Exports Program sunset and the $135 billion exposure cap, per CRS. S. 3772 would extend them 10 years.

The Senate Banking Committee holds a full committee hearing titled 'Export-Import Bank Reauthorization' (the committee's hearing listing gives the title only; its listing for later 2026 hearings through 2026-10-01 shows no further Export-Import Bank hearing, and markups were not checked).
timeline.source: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

timeline.event: CRS updates its EXIM report: the charter sunsets 2026-12-31; no 119th Congress bill to abolish the Bank is identified; the FY2027 request seeks a $200 million program budget, up from $20 million.
Chairman Jovanovic outlines EXIM's role in securing supply chains and rebuilding the industrial base (EXIM news item, title only reviewed).

Executive Order 14415 on defense supply chains is signed (published 2026-07-23); section 6 states the order does not affect Project Vault or acquisitions from foreign projects that EXIM finances, guarantees or insures.

EXIM publishes notice of a pending long-term loan or guarantee above $100 million for Astranis Space Technologies, to finance components for domestic satellite production; it is one of several such notices in 2026.

The House Financial Services Committee's full committee markups of 2026-05-13, 2026-06-30 and 2026-09-16 list no measure concerning the Export-Import Bank (the 2026-09-16 agenda is at the linked page); the enrolled Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500, signed 2026-09-02) contains no Export-Import Bank provision, so the charter remains set to expire on 2026-12-31 (other House committee markups were not checked).

EXIM reports that its Chairman joined the President in the Oval Office to announce a planned $15 billion steel plant in Iowa, after EXIM's Board approved a $770 million direct loan the week before for the supplier iron ore mine in Minnesota; the release quotes the Chairman only and records no presidential statement about EXIM's role or reauthorization.

title: Abolish the Export-Import Bank rather than reauthorize or expand it
uncertainties: Pass 5: S. 3772's text, H.R. 6500's enrolled text, three House Financial Services markup agendas, the Senate Banking hearing listing and EXIM's newsroom were read; no statement by the President or Commerce Secretary about abolishing or keeping EXIM was found beyond budget and order texts, and EXIM's 2026-09-28 release records none. The last part of the CRS report was not read. Whether Congress reauthorizes EXIM before 2026-12-31 is unknown. The 'diverged' label rests on the contrast between the abolition recommendation and the administration's expansion; a reader favoring the Hazelton essay would instead see these actions as consistent with that essay. The exim.gov news page date is the newest item listed, not a publication date for the page.
